q: In which year BC did the Athenians defeat the Persians at the Battle of Marathon?
x: Legend says a messenger ran about 25 miles to Athens with news of victory, which inspired the modern marathon race.

q: Which 1494 treaty divided newly found lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal?
x: The line ran west of the Cape Verde Islands, which is why Brazil ended up Portuguese-speaking while most of Latin America speaks Spanish.

q: At which 1571 naval battle did a Holy League fleet defeat the Ottoman navy?
x: The clash off western Greece was among the largest galley battles ever fought. Miguel de Cervantes was wounded in it.

q: Which Polish king led the relief army that broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683?
x: Sobieski led what is considered one of history's largest cavalry charges, and the defeat marked the start of Ottoman decline in central Europe.

q: Which East India Company commander won the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
x: Clive's force was far smaller than the Bengal army, but secret deals with its commanders helped decide the outcome.

q: In which year did Napoleon win the Battle of Austerlitz, his famous "Battle of the Three Emperors"?
x: He defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army on the first anniversary of his coronation, December 2, 1805.

q: In which year did Napoleon launch his invasion of Russia?
x: He crossed the Niemen River with perhaps 450,000 men in June. Only a small fraction survived the retreat that winter.

q: Which 1840 treaty was signed between the British Crown and Maori chiefs in New Zealand?
x: The treaty has English and Maori versions that differ in meaning, which has been the subject of debate and legal claims ever since.

q: Who led the Taiping Rebellion in China from 1850 to 1864?
x: Hong claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus. The rebellion is one of the deadliest civil wars in history, with tens of millions dead.

q: Which US cavalry commander was killed at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876?
x: Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors under leaders including Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse won a rare, decisive victory over the 7th Cavalry.

q: The explosion of which US battleship in Havana harbor in 1898 helped spark the Spanish-American War?
x: "Remember the Maine" became a popular slogan. A later investigation concluded the cause was probably an internal fire rather than an enemy attack.

q: In which US city was the 1905 treaty ending the Russo-Japanese War signed?
x: President Theodore Roosevelt mediated the talks and won the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize for the effort.

q: The 1915 Gallipoli campaign was an Allied attempt to force which strait?
x: The campaign failed after eight months. It became a founding moment for the national identities of Australia and New Zealand.

q: Which 1918 treaty took Soviet Russia out of World War I?
x: Russia gave up huge territories, including Ukraine and the Baltic states, but Germany's own defeat later in 1918 voided the treaty.

q: In which French forest was the armistice ending World War I signed in November 1918?
x: The signing took place in a railway carriage. In 1940 Hitler made France sign its surrender in the very same carriage.

q: In which city did Hitler lead the failed Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923?
x: The coup attempt failed within a day. Hitler wrote Mein Kampf during the months he spent in prison afterward.

q: The 1938 Munich Agreement forced which country to hand the Sudetenland to Germany?
x: Czechoslovakia was not invited to the conference. Neville Chamberlain returned to Britain promising "peace for our time."

q: What was the code name of Germany's 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union?
x: Launched on June 22, 1941, it involved over three million Axis troops along a front of roughly 1,800 miles.

q: Near which Pacific atoll did the US Navy win a decisive battle in June 1942?
x: US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese carriers, and Japan never regained the initiative in the Pacific.

q: In February 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at which Crimean resort?
x: The "Big Three" discussed the postwar order, including the division of Germany and the creation of the United Nations.

q: Which Egyptian president nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956?
x: Britain, France and Israel invaded in response, but US and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw.

q: What was the name of the dog sent into orbit aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957?
x: Laika was a stray found on the streets of Moscow. The craft was not designed to return, and she was the first animal to orbit Earth.

q: In 1975, the US Apollo spacecraft docked in orbit with which Soviet craft?
x: The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project was a symbol of détente, and the crews shared meals and exchanged gifts in space.

q: Which Soviet space station was launched in 1986 and orbited until 2001?
x: Mir means "peace" or "world" in Russian. It was assembled in orbit over a decade and hosted more than 100 astronauts.

q: Which ruler founded the Akkadian Empire around 2300 BC, creating one of the first empires?
x: Sargon is said to have been born to humble parents and set adrift on a river in a basket, a story later echoed in other legends.

q: Which Assyrian king assembled a great library of clay tablets at Nineveh?
x: His library held tens of thousands of tablets, including the Epic of Gilgamesh, and was rediscovered in the 1850s.

q: Ramses II fought the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BC against which empire?
x: The battle led to the first known peace treaty between two great powers, copies of which survive in both Egyptian and Hittite.

q: Which Mediterranean island was the center of the Minoan civilization?
x: The Minoans built the palace at Knossos, and the myth of the labyrinth and the Minotaur may echo its maze-like layout.

q: Which British archaeologist began excavating the palace of Knossos in 1900?
x: Evans coined the name "Minoan" after the legendary King Minos, and his partial reconstructions of the site remain controversial.

q: Which German amateur archaeologist excavated the site of Troy at Hisarlik in the 1870s?
x: Schliemann dug so quickly and roughly that he probably destroyed layers belonging to the Trojan War era.

q: Which early Mesoamerican civilization is famous for carving colossal stone heads?
x: The Olmec flourished on Mexico's Gulf Coast from about 1200 BC, and some of their heads weigh over 20 tons.

q: Which ruler transformed Cusco into the center of the Inca Empire in the mid-1400s?
x: His name means "he who transforms the earth." He is credited with building Machu Picchu as a royal estate.

q: The ancient Mississippian city of Cahokia lies across the river from which modern US city?
x: Around AD 1100 Cahokia may have had 10,000 to 20,000 people, and its Monks Mound is the largest earthen structure in North America.

q: Which Mughal emperor, grandson of Babur, ruled from 1556 to 1605?
x: Akbar was famous for religious tolerance and for hosting scholars of many faiths at his court.

q: Which ruler founded the Mughal Empire after winning the First Battle of Panipat in 1526?
x: Babur descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, and he used gunpowder weapons to defeat a much larger army.

q: Which Mauryan emperor, after the bloody Kalinga war, spread his edicts on stone pillars across India?
x: Ashoka's lion capital from Sarnath is now the national emblem of India, and his pillars are among the oldest surviving Indian inscriptions.

q: Which Khmer king built the temple of Angkor Wat in the 12th century?
x: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world and appears on the flag of Cambodia.

q: Great Zimbabwe, a medieval stone city in southern Africa, was built by ancestors of which people?
x: The site grew rich on gold and cattle between about 1100 and 1450. Modern Zimbabwe takes its name from the ruins.

q: Which Phoenician city is traditionally credited with founding Carthage?
x: Tradition dates the founding to 814 BC and credits Queen Dido, who according to legend outwitted a local ruler to gain land.

q: At which battle in 202 BC did Scipio Africanus defeat Hannibal?
x: The victory ended the Second Punic War and made Rome the dominant power of the western Mediterranean.

q: Who led the great slave revolt against Rome that began in 73 BC?
x: The revolt began with about 70 gladiators escaping from a school in Capua and grew to tens of thousands of followers.

q: Which queen of the Iceni led an uprising against Roman rule in Britain around AD 60?
x: Her forces burned Londinium, Verulamium and Camulodunum before being defeated. A statue of her stands by Westminster Bridge in London.

q: Which Roman emperor divided the empire's rule among four co-rulers in AD 293?
x: The system, called the Tetrarchy, was meant to make the huge empire easier to defend. Diocletian later retired to grow cabbages.

q: Which Germanic leader destroyed three Roman legions at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9?
x: The defeat convinced Emperor Augustus to stop expanding east of the Rhine. He is said to have cried out for his lost legions.

q: Which Visigothic king sacked the city of Rome in AD 410?
x: It was the first time in about 800 years that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy, and it shocked the Roman world.

q: Which Byzantine emperor oversaw the building of the Hagia Sophia, completed in 537?
x: The great church was built in under six years and, for nearly a thousand years, was the largest cathedral in the world.

q: Who commanded the Frankish forces at the Battle of Tours in 732?
x: Charles Martel was the grandfather of Charlemagne, and his name means "Charles the Hammer."

q: To which Italian city did the Western Roman emperors move their capital in AD 402?
x: Ravenna's marshes made it easier to defend than Milan, and it later housed splendid mosaics from the Byzantine period.

q: Which Roman emperor wrote the philosophical work Meditations?
x: He wrote it as private notes while on military campaigns. It is regarded as a classic of Stoic philosophy.

q: Which city did Caliph al-Mansur found in 762 as the Abbasid capital?
x: Baghdad's round design earned it the nickname "Round City." It became a center of learning with the House of Wisdom.

q: The word "algorithm" comes from the name of which 9th-century Persian scholar?
x: His book on calculation also gave us the word "algebra," from the Arabic al-jabr.

q: Which king of Wessex defeated the Danes at the Battle of Edington in 878?
x: Alfred is the only English monarch called "the Great" and is credited with founding the English navy and promoting literacy.

q: Which Danish king ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the early 1000s?
x: A story says Cnut sat by the sea and ordered the tide to stop, to show his courtiers that even a king has limits.

q: At which September 1066 battle did an English army beat a Norwegian invasion?
x: The English victory in Yorkshire came just three weeks before the Norman landing in the south.

q: In 1347, plague-bearing ships first reached Europe at which Sicilian port?
x: Genoese trading ships fleeing the Black Sea carried the disease. By 1351 it had swept across nearly all of Europe.

q: Who led the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
x: The rebels marched on London after a poll tax was imposed. Tyler was killed during talks with the young King Richard II.

q: Which Parliamentarian became Lord Protector of England in 1653?
x: After the execution of Charles I, England was a republic. Cromwell refused the crown but held near-royal powers until 1658.

q: Which Dutch prince became King of England after the Glorious Revolution of 1688?
x: William ruled jointly with his wife Mary II, and the revolution was largely bloodless in England, which is why it is called "Glorious."

q: At the 1709 Battle of Poltava, Peter the Great's Russia decisively defeated which country?
x: The victory over Charles XII ended Sweden's days as a great power and made Russia the leading force in northern Europe.

q: Which Habsburg ruler governed Austria, Hungary and Bohemia from 1740 to 1780?
x: She had 16 children, and her youngest daughter, Marie Antoinette, became Queen of France.

q: Which Jacobin leader dominated the Committee of Public Safety during the Reign of Terror?
x: Robespierre himself was overthrown in July 1794, ending the Terror, which had claimed thousands of lives.

q: For which event was the Eiffel Tower built in 1889?
x: The fair marked the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution, and the tower was meant to be dismantled after 20 years.

q: In which year was the Great Exhibition held in London's Crystal Palace?
x: Prince Albert helped organize it. Over six million visits were made, and its profits helped fund London's great museums.

q: Who made the first airplane flight across the English Channel in 1909?
x: Bleriot's flight took about 36 minutes and earned a prize of 1,000 pounds from a British newspaper.

q: Which scientist discovered penicillin in 1928?
x: Fleming noticed that mold had killed bacteria on a forgotten culture dish. Florey and Chain later turned it into a usable drug.

q: In which US state did the airship Hindenburg burst into flames in 1937?
x: The disaster at Lakehurst, filmed and broadcast on radio, ended the era of passenger airships. Most people aboard survived.

q: Who led Czechoslovakia's reform movement known as the Prague Spring in 1968?
x: Dubcek promoted "socialism with a human face." Warsaw Pact troops invaded in August 1968 to end the reforms.

q: In which year were the Voyager 1 and 2 space probes launched?
x: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 and is the most distant human-made object, carrying a golden record of Earth's sounds.

q: Which Athenian lawgiver's reforms around 594 BC laid groundwork for democracy by cancelling debts?
x: Solon freed Athenians who had been enslaved for debt. His rival Draco, by contrast, gave us the word "draconian."

q: What was the name of Alexander the Great's famous horse?
x: Alexander tamed the horse as a boy by turning it toward the sun, since it was frightened of its own shadow.

q: Which Persian king did Alexander defeat at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BC?
x: Darius fled the field and was killed by his own officers soon after, leaving Alexander master of the Persian Empire.

q: Which dynasty, founded by a general of Alexander the Great, ruled Egypt until Cleopatra?
x: Ptolemy I founded the Library of Alexandria. Cleopatra VII was the last of the line and the only one said to speak Egyptian.

q: Which calendar did Julius Caesar introduce in 45 BC?
x: It had 365 days and a leap day every four years. It was off by a few minutes a year, and by 1582 the error had reached about ten days.

q: Which pope introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582?
x: To fix the drift, ten days were skipped. In Catholic countries October 4 was followed by October 15, 1582.

q: Which Moroccan traveler journeyed across much of the Old World in the 1300s?
x: He traveled about 75,000 miles over nearly 30 years, visiting places from West Africa to China.

q: Which Portuguese prince sponsored voyages down Africa's coast in the early 1400s?
x: Henry never sailed far himself. He supported navigation research and ships that paved the way for later explorers.

q: Which Portuguese navigator was the first European to round the southern tip of Africa, in 1488?
x: Dias named it the Cape of Storms. King John II renamed it the Cape of Good Hope to inspire hope for a route to India.

q: Which Portuguese navigator reached Brazil in 1500?
x: Cabral was heading for India with a large fleet when his ships were blown far west and he claimed the land for Portugal.

q: Whose first name inspired the naming of the Americas?
x: Mapmaker Martin Waldseemuller used the name America on his 1507 world map after Vespucci argued the lands were a new continent.

q: Which French explorer sailed up the St. Lawrence River in 1534 and claimed the land for France?
x: Cartier heard the Iroquoian word "kanata," meaning village, and it eventually became the name Canada.

q: Which priest launched the 1810 Mexican War of Independence with the Grito de Dolores?
x: Mexico celebrates the cry on September 16. Hidalgo was captured and executed in 1811, but the movement carried on.

q: Who declared Brazil independent from Portugal in 1822?
x: Pedro was the son of Portugal's king, and he became Brazil's first emperor after declaring independence with the cry "Independence or death!"

q: In which year did Canada become a self-governing dominion through Confederation?
x: The new country began with four provinces: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. July 1 is now Canada Day.

q: In which year did the Australian colonies federate into the Commonwealth of Australia?
x: Federation came on January 1, 1901. Canberra, chosen as a compromise capital between Sydney and Melbourne, was founded in 1913.

q: Which country became the first self-governing nation to give women the vote in national elections, in 1893?
x: Suffragist Kate Sheppard led the campaign, and her petition had nearly 32,000 signatures. She appears on New Zealand's 10-dollar note.

q: Which Russian tsar freed the serfs in 1861?
x: Known as the "Tsar Liberator," Alexander II freed an estimated 23 million serfs. He was assassinated in 1881.

q: Who founded the Tokugawa shogunate in Japan in 1603?
x: His family ruled Japan in relative peace for over 250 years, until the Meiji Restoration of 1868.

q: Which Korean admiral used armored "turtle ships" against Japanese invasions in the 1590s?
x: Yi won all of his major naval battles, and his statue stands in the center of Seoul today.

q: Which Korean king oversaw the creation of the Hangul alphabet in 1443?
x: Hangul was designed so that ordinary people could learn it quickly. Korea celebrates it with a national holiday.

q: What was Genghis Khan's birth name?
x: He was given the title Genghis Khan, roughly "universal ruler," at a gathering of Mongol tribes in 1206.

q: Which dynasty's forces defeated the Mongols at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260?
x: It was among the first major defeats of the Mongol army and halted their advance toward Egypt.

q: Which short-lived Chinese dynasty, from 581 to 618, linked rivers by building the Grand Canal?
x: The Grand Canal grew to be the longest artificial waterway in the world and carried grain from the south to the north for centuries.

q: Who was the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right?
x: She ruled from 690 to 705 during the Tang era and founded her own short dynasty, the Zhou.

q: In which year was the Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded?
x: The VOC is often called the first publicly traded company, and at its peak it was among the richest companies in history.

q: Who invented dynamite in 1867?
x: Nobel's will left his fortune to create the Nobel Prizes. A newspaper's mistaken obituary for him reportedly influenced the decision.

q: Which 1783 treaty formally ended the American Revolutionary War?
x: Britain recognized American independence and agreed to borders reaching west to the Mississippi River.

q: Who was the first monarch of England's Tudor dynasty?
x: Henry VII won the crown at Bosworth in 1485 and strengthened royal finances. He united the houses of Lancaster and York by marrying Elizabeth of York.

q: Which Roman emperor began building a wall across northern Britain in AD 122?
x: The wall ran about 73 miles coast to coast. Antoninus Pius later built another, the Antonine Wall, further north in Scotland.

q: Which Aztec ruler was emperor when Hernan Cortes arrived in 1519?
x: Moctezuma welcomed the Spaniards into Tenochtitlan, and he died in 1520. Cuauhtemoc, his successor's successor, led the last defense.

q: Which Greek writer is often called the "Father of History"?
x: His Histories, about the Greco-Persian Wars, mix careful inquiry with colorful stories, and the Greek word historia means "inquiry."
